title: The booking core in code
idea: Building the core means writing `BookingService` and its repositories so search, book and cancel run end to end in memory, before any database or HTTP.
points: Build inside out: repositories and policy first, then the service that uses them.
In-memory repositories with `Map` stand in for a database behind the same methods.
The service orchestrates: it asks, decides and saves, but stores nothing itself.
Constructor injection hands in every collaborator, so tests can swap any of them.

messages.label: book('e1', 'r2', 9, 10)
messages.note: An employee asks for room `r2` from 9 to 10.

messages.label: forRoom('r2')
messages.note: The service loads only that room's bookings, not every booking.

messages.label: existing bookings
messages.note: The repository returns a list; the service does not know how it is stored.

messages.label: conflicts(slot, existing)
messages.note: The overlap decision is delegated to the injected policy.

messages.label: false
messages.note: No clash, so the booking can go ahead.

messages.label: save(booking)
messages.note: Only now does the service create an id and save the booking.

messages.label: booking
messages.note: The caller gets the saved booking back, with its id for a later cancel.

code.title: Core modules, in memory
code.caption: All three use cases run with no database. Book `r1` for 9 to 10 too, and run again.

walk.text: `InMemoryRoomRepository` keeps rooms in a private `Map` and lists them.
`InMemoryBookingRepository` saves, finds, removes, and lists one room's bookings.
`StrictOverlapPolicy` implements `ConflictPolicy`: half-open slots, so back-to-back is allowed.
The service receives its collaborators. `searchFree` filters by capacity, then asks the policy.
`book` checks first and creates an id only for a booking that is saved.
`cancel` lets only the employee who booked remove the booking.
Wire the parts by hand and run each use case, including two failures.

pitfalls: Do not put `Map` storage inside `BookingService`; keep storage behind a repository.
Check for conflicts before generating ids or side effects, not after.
Avoid `new` for collaborators inside the service; inject them through the constructor.

quiz.q: Why does `BookingService` take its repositories and policy as constructor arguments?
options: Because JavaScript classes cannot use `new` inside methods
So a test can pass in fakes or another policy
So the service can store bookings itself
quiz.why: Injected collaborators can be swapped without editing the service, so tests and new rules plug in from outside.

takeaway: Make every use case run in memory before adding storage or HTTP.

starters: Why use in-memory repositories before a real database?
How would two concurrent bookings for the same room be handled?
Should searchFree live in BookingService or RoomRepository?
